items.stem: What is the nth term of 16, 24, 32, 40, …?
items.markingKey: D. Difference 8 → 8n; first term 16 = 8(1) + 8.

items.stem: A student claims: "The nth term of 4, 7, 10, 13, … is n + 3 because you add 3 each time." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Adding 3 each time gives 3n; 3(1) + 1 = 4, so the nth term is 3n + 1.
items.markingKey: Adding 3 each time gives 3n; 3(1) + 1 = 4, so the nth term is 3n + 1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why an nth term rule is more useful than a term-to-term rule for finding the 100th term.
items.answer: The nth term gives the 100th term directly by substituting n = 100, without working out the 99 terms before it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The nth term gives the 100th term directly by substituting n = 100, without working out the 99 terms before it. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Is 105 a term of the sequence 1, 3, 5, 7, …? Show how you decide.
items.answer: Yes: 2n − 1 = 105 gives n = 53
items.markingKey: nth term 2n − 1 (A1); solve 2n − 1 = 105 (M1); conclusion with reason (R1).

items.stem: For the sequence −1, −6, −11, −16, … find (a) the nth term, (b) the 80th term.

Ingrid has CHF 74 saved after week 1 and adds CHF 8 every week, so the totals form the sequence 74, 82, 90, … (a) Find the nth term. (b) Find the total after 37 weeks. (c) In which week does the total first exceed CHF 470? (d) Explain why this is a linear sequence.
items.answer: (a) 8n + 66 (b) CHF 362 (c) week 51 (d) the same amount CHF 8 is added each week (constant difference)
items.markingKey: (a) 8n + 66 (b) CHF 362 (c) week 51 (d) the same amount CHF 8 is added each week (constant difference). Pattern described and generalised (B: M1 A1); rule used for a far term and inverted (A1 A1); justification (R1 C1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An ordered list of numbers that follow a rule"?
items.answer: sequence
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of sequence.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the nth term of a linear sequence with common difference d starts with dn.
items.answer: Each step adds d, so the terms go up in the same way as the d-times table, dn; the constant adjusts for the starting value.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each step adds d, so the terms go up in the same way as the d-times table, dn; the constant adjusts for the starting value. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ingrid says the nth term of 14, 19, 24, 29, … is n + 5. Explain why this is wrong and find the correct nth term.
items.answer: n + 5 gives 6, 7, … which go up by 1, not 5; correct nth term 5n + 9.
items.markingKey: Test of n = 2 or the difference shows the error (R1); 5n + 9 (A1).

items.answer: No: 9n + 3 = 94 gives n = 10.11, not a whole number

items.stem: A student claims: "The sequence 2, 6, 18, 54 is linear because it goes up each time." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The differences 4, 12, 36 are not constant (each term is multiplied by 3), so it is not linear.

items.stem: Square tiles are arranged in patterns: pattern 1 has 9 tiles, pattern 2 has 14, pattern 3 has 19. (a) Find a formula for the number of tiles in pattern n. (b) How many tiles are in pattern 24? (c) Which pattern uses exactly 159 tiles? (d) Explain why no pattern uses 125 tiles.
items.answer: (a) 5n + 4 (b) 124 (c) pattern 31 (d) 5n + 4 = 125 gives n = 24 + 1/5, not a whole number

items.stem: Investigate the family of lines y = mx − 1. (a) For m = 1, 2 and 3 find where each line crosses the x-axis. (b) Describe the pattern. (c) Find, in terms of m, where y = mx − 1 crosses the x-axis.
items.answer: (a) x = 1, 1/2, 1/3 (b) the x-intercept moves towards 0 as m increases (c) x = 1/m
items.markingKey: (a) x = 1, 1/2, 1/3 (b) the x-intercept moves towards 0 as m increases (c) x = 1/m. Gradient and equation found (M1 A1); point tested or pattern generalised (B: M1 A1); clear notation (C1).

items.stem: Rafael has GH₵61 saved after week 1 and adds GH₵8 every week, so the totals form the sequence 61, 69, 77, … (a) Find the nth term. (b) Find the total after 35 weeks. (c) In which week does the total first exceed GH₵441? (d) Explain why this is a linear sequence.
items.answer: (a) 8n + 53 (b) GH₵333 (c) week 49 (d) the same amount GH₵8 is added each week (constant difference)
items.markingKey: (a) 8n + 53 (b) GH₵333 (c) week 49 (d) the same amount GH₵8 is added each week (constant difference). Pattern described and generalised (B: M1 A1); rule used for a far term and inverted (A1 A1); justification (R1 C1).

items.stem: Complete a table of values for y = 4x + 0 for x = −2 to 3. (a) Plot the graph and state where it crosses the y-axis. (b) Find the value of x when y = 20. (c) Explain how the table shows that the points lie on a straight line.
items.answer: (a) y-values −8, −4, 0, 4, 8, 12; crosses the y-axis at (0, 0) (b) x = 5 (c) y increases by 4 for every increase of 1 in x (constant difference)
items.markingKey: (a) y-values −8, −4, 0, 4, 8, 12; crosses the y-axis at (0, 0) (b) x = 5 (c) y increases by 4 for every increase of 1 in x (constant difference). Coordinates and table used correctly (M1 A1); calculation (A1); pattern or feature described with correct notation (B/C: R1 C1).

items.stem: Two bike-hire companies in Lisbon: Company A charges €3 plus €1.76 per km; Company B charges €11 plus €1.28 per km. (a) Write an equation for each and describe their graphs. (b) Find the distance at which the costs are equal. (c) Advise a rider making a 21 km trip.
items.answer: (a) A: C = 3 + 1.76d, B: C = 11 + 1.28d – straight lines, A has the greater gradient, B the greater intercept (b) d = 16.67 km (c) B is cheaper for trips longer than 16.67 km, so choose B
items.markingKey: (a) A: C = 3 + 1.76d, B: C = 11 + 1.28d – straight lines, A has the greater gradient, B the greater intercept (b) d = 16.67 km (c) B is cheaper for trips longer than 16.67 km, so choose B. Linear models/graphs set up (M1 A1); intersection found algebraically or graphically (M1 A1); interpretation in context (D: R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gradient"?
options: A measure of the steepness of a line: the change in y divided by the change in x
The point (0, 0) where the axes cross
A table of chosen x-values and the matching y-values calculated from a rule, used to plot a graph
One of the four regions into which the x- and y-axes divide the coordinate plane
items.answer: A measure of the steepness of a line: the change in y divided by the change in x
items.markingKey: A. "gradient" is a measure of the steepness of a line: the change in y divided by the change in x.

items.stem: Define the term "term-to-term rule".
items.answer: The rule that tells you how to get from one term of a sequence to the next
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the rule that tells you how to get from one term of a sequence to the next. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "origin"?
options: The point (0, 0) where the axes cross
A straight-line graph used to change between two units, such as currencies or temperature scales
A table of chosen x-values and the matching y-values calculated from a rule, used to plot a graph
A measure of the steepness of a line: the change in y divided by the change in x
items.answer: The point (0, 0) where the axes cross
items.markingKey: A. "origin" is the point (0, 0) where the axes cross.

items.stem: Ana’s distance–time graph has three sections: steep upward, then horizontal, then less steep upward. Write a short story that matches the graph and explain how you used the gradients.
items.answer: E.g. runs quickly to a bus stop, waits, then walks the rest of the way more slowly; steep = fast, horizontal = stopped, less steep = slower.
items.markingKey: Each section matched to a plausible motion (A1 A1); gradient ↔ speed explained (R1).

items.stem: Explain why the lines y = −5x and y = −5x + 3 never meet.
items.answer: Both have gradient −5 but different intercepts, so they are parallel and distinct.
items.markingKey: Equal gradients (R1); different intercepts ⇒ no intersection (R1).

items.stem: Isabel says the nth term of 9, 16, 23, 30, … is n + 7. Explain why this is wrong and find the correct nth term.
items.answer: n + 7 gives 8, 9, … which go up by 1, not 7; correct nth term 7n + 2.
items.markingKey: Test of n = 2 or the difference shows the error (R1); 7n + 2 (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "To plot (4, −1), go 4 up and 1 left." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The x-coordinate comes first: 4 right, then 1 down.
items.markingKey: The x-coordinate comes first: 4 right, then 1 down. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a steeper section of a distance–time graph means a higher speed.
items.answer: A steeper line covers more distance in the same time, and speed is distance ÷ time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A steeper line covers more distance in the same time, and speed is distance ÷ time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the lines y = 4x and y = 4x + 3 never meet.
items.answer: Both have gradient 4 but different intercepts, so they are parallel and distinct.
items.markingKey: Equal gradients (R1); different intercepts ⇒ no intersection (R1).

items.stem: Mateo writes: "The nth term of 4, 7, 10, 13, … is n + 3 because you add 3 each time." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Adding 3 each time gives 3n; 3(1) + 1 = 4, so the nth term is 3n + 1.
items.markingKey: Adding 3 each time gives 3n; 3(1) + 1 = 4, so the nth term is 3n + 1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Complete a table of values for y = −2x + 6 for x = −3, −1, 0, 2, 4, and write the coordinates of the points to plot.
items.markingKey: Each y found by substitution (M1); all correct (A1 A1).

items.stem: A conversion graph passes through (0, 0) and (100, 113) for euros (x) and US dollars (y). Use it to convert 20 euros to US dollars, and 226 US dollars to euros.
items.answer: 22.6 US dollars; 200 euros

items.stem: State the gradient and the y-intercept of the line y = −9 + 3x.
items.answer: gradient 3, y-intercept (0, −9)
items.markingKey: Rearrange to y = mx + c if needed (M1); gradient 3 (A1); intercept (0, −9) (A1).

items.stem: For the sequence −3, −9, −15, −21, … find (a) the nth term, (b) the 67th term.
A parallelogram has vertices A(−2, −4), B(2, −4) and C(3, 3). Find D so that ABCD is a parallelogram, and state the quadrant(s) in which A lies.
items.answer: D(−1, 3); A is in the third quadrant
items.markingKey: Translation from B to C applied to A (M1); D(−1, 3) (A1); quadrant of A stated from signs (A1).

items.stem: "A taxi fare graph that starts at 3 on the cost axis shows direct proportion." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It does not pass through the origin, so cost is not directly proportional to distance (there is a fixed charge).
items.markingKey: It does not pass through the origin, so cost is not directly proportional to distance (there is a fixed charge). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Investigate the family of lines y = mx − 4. (a) For m = 1, 2 and 3 find where each line crosses the x-axis. (b) Describe the pattern. (c) Find, in terms of m, where y = mx − 4 crosses the x-axis.
items.answer: (a) x = 4, 2, 4/3 (b) the x-intercept moves towards 0 as m increases (c) x = 4/m
items.markingKey: (a) x = 4, 2, 4/3 (b) the x-intercept moves towards 0 as m increases (c) x = 4/m. Gradient and equation found (M1 A1); point tested or pattern generalised (B: M1 A1); clear notation (C1).

items.stem: Square tiles are arranged in patterns: pattern 1 has 3 tiles, pattern 2 has 5, pattern 3 has 7. (a) Find a formula for the number of tiles in pattern n. (b) How many tiles are in pattern 16? (c) Which pattern uses exactly 47 tiles? (d) Explain why no pattern uses 34 tiles.
items.answer: (a) 2n + 1 (b) 33 (c) pattern 23 (d) 2n + 1 = 34 gives n = 16 + 1/2, not a whole number
items.markingKey: (a) 2n + 1 (b) 33 (c) pattern 23 (d) 2n + 1 = 34 gives n = 16 + 1/2, not a whole number. Pattern described and generalised (B: M1 A1); rule used for a far term and inverted (A1 A1); justification (R1 C1).

items.stem: A map of a park in Mumbai uses a grid in kilometres. The café is at (−4, 2), the lake at (3, 2) and the gate at (3, −5). (a) Describe the route café → lake → gate in terms of distances and directions. (b) Find the total distance walked. (c) Find the coordinates of a bench exactly halfway between the café and the gate.
items.answer: (a) 7 km east, then 7 km south (b) 14 km (c) (−1/2, −3/2)
items.markingKey: (a) 7 km east, then 7 km south (b) 14 km (c) (−1/2, −3/2). Coordinates and table used correctly (M1 A1); calculation (A1); pattern or feature described with correct notation (B/C: R1 C1).

items.stem: Two bike-hire companies in Kuala Lumpur: Company A charges RM3 plus RM2.45 per km; Company B charges RM9 plus RM1.86 per km. (a) Write an equation for each and describe their graphs. (b) Find the distance at which the costs are equal. (c) Advise a rider making a 15 km trip.
items.answer: (a) A: C = 3 + 2.45d, B: C = 9 + 1.86d – straight lines, A has the greater gradient, B the greater intercept (b) d = 10.17 km (c) B is cheaper for trips longer than 10.17 km, so choose B
items.markingKey: (a) A: C = 3 + 2.45d, B: C = 9 + 1.86d – straight lines, A has the greater gradient, B the greater intercept (b) d = 10.17 km (c) B is cheaper for trips longer than 10.17 km, so choose B. Linear models/graphs set up (M1 A1); intersection found algebraically or graphically (M1 A1); interpretation in context (D: R1).
